newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan president kicks off high-profile war games.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan president kicks off high-profile war games.

text.p: President Lee Teng-hui on Monday reviewed a display of Taiwan's beefed-up arsenal, kicking off high-profile war games seen by some as provocative ahead of China's takeover of Hong Kong.

Bolstering Taipei's message of defiance, Lee's tour of two military bases was aired live on Taiwan television and witnessed by 200 foreign reporters -- ensuring the message would resound across the Taiwan strait to Taiwan-watchers in the mainland.
Taiwan has said the timing of its two-day "Chinese glory" drills, announced a year ago, had nothing to do with Britain's midnight, June 30, handover of Hong Kong to Beijing.

Commanders made clear, however, that they had everything to do with mainland China and its intensifying drive to isolate the exiled Republic of China, which retreated to Taiwan after losing a civil war to the communists in 1949.

"This exercise can show our countrymen the military's accomplishment in breaking through the obstacles of military procurement and their success in domestic weaponry research and development," the defence ministry said in a statement.
Beijing, which views Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as a renegade province, has warned other countries against arming the island in its drive to bring it under mainland rule.

Lee started the day at southern Taiwan's Tainan air base, where he inspected a host of high-tech imported arms, including U.S. F-16 and French Mirage 2000-5 jet fighters, AH-1W attack helicopters and OH-58D surveillance helicopters.

The most innocuous-looking yet sophisticated weapons on show were the long, boxy truck-mounted launchers containing U.S.-made Patriot antimissile missiles -- procured to shoot down incoming missiles in the event of attack by mainland China.
Lee nodded in satisfaction as he passed the drab green unmarked Patriots -- which at US$1 million each were not scheduled to be fired in Tuesday's live-fire war games.
The Patriots, along with advanced U.S. Hawk missiles and a range of home-made, anchor Taiwan's defence network.
Also displayed were some of the 300 old M60A3 tanks that Taiwan bought on the cheap from the U.S. scrap heap -- only to upgrade them with top-flight electronic anti-aircraft systems.
The only gunfire on the exercises' largely ceremonial first day was a 21-gun salute fired off for Lee as he arrived for the day's second event, a naval review at Tsoying naval base.

Lee motored past 4,200 officers from 44 vessels, including Knox-class frigates leased from the United States, radar-evading Lafayette "stealth" frigates from France, Dutch-made submarines and local missile frigates.
The exercises have been seen by some as provocative because their timing comes so close to Hong Kong's handover.
Yet Beijing has declined to be drawn.

The official Xinhua news agency on Sunday issued a commentary that hailed Hong Kong's return to China under a "one country, two systems" model of local autonomy as an example for Taiwan's own "reunification with the motherland".
The commentary made no mention of Taiwan's war games.
Similarly, China's spokesmen have skipped chances to assail the drills, reinforcing analysts' belief that Beijing wants to avoid mudslinging that might spoil Hong Kong's shining moment.
Beijing also has declined to comment on unconfirmed Hong Kong reports that it was planning "counterbalancing" manoeuvres, something military analysts called unlikely.
Washington gave voice to international concerns about the timing of Taiwan's drills, urging the sides on June 11 not to stage exercises during the run-up to Hong Kong's handover.
